## What you will learn

- How a crop model grows a crop each day: photosynthesis, respiration, and how the new mass is shared
  between leaves, stems, roots, pods and seeds.
- What a DSSAT weather file holds, how to check it, how to convert data from other units, and how much the
  simulated crop depends on each weather variable.
- Which files make up the minimum data set of a run and how DSSAT names them.
- The difference between species, ecotype and cultivar coefficients, and how day length and cultivar
  coefficients set when a soybean flowers and matures.

The example is a soybean experiment from Gainesville, Florida, in 1979 (`UFGA7901`, cultivar Bragg),
shipped with DSSAT [@csmdata]. It has two treatments, irrigated and rainfed, both planted on 19 June. Soybean
is simulated by CROPGRO, the grain legume model of DSSAT-CSM [@jones2003].

## 1. Growth processes

### The daily carbon balance

Each day CROPGRO computes **gross photosynthesis**, subtracts **maintenance respiration** (the cost of
keeping existing tissue alive, part proportional to the plant's mass and part to the day's photosynthesis,
[`RESPIR.for:54`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/RESPIR.for#L54)),
and converts what is left into new tissue, losing **growth respiration** in the conversion. What is added
to the crop that day is the **crop growth rate**:

\[
\frac{dW}{dt} = E\,(P_g - R_m), \qquad R_m = r_o\,W + r_p\,P_g
\]

with \(W\) the crop's dry weight, \(P_g\) gross photosynthesis, \(R_m\) maintenance respiration, \(E\) the
conversion efficiency of carbohydrate into tissue (one minus the growth respiration share), and \(r_o\), \(r_p\)
temperature-dependent coefficients (`RO`, `RP` in `RESPIR.for`).

```{ojs}
viewof cTrt = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Irrigated", 1], ["Rainfed", 2]]), {value: 1, label: "Treatment"})
```

```{ojs}
cLong = carbon.filter(d => d.TRNO === cTrt).flatMap(d => [
  {DAP: d.DAP, v: d.PHAD, term: "gross photosynthesis"}, {DAP: d.DAP, v: d.MRAD, term: "maintenance respiration"},
  {DAP: d.DAP, v: d.GRAD, term: "growth respiration"}, {DAP: d.DAP, v: d.CGRD, term: "crop growth rate"}])
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 340, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: "g CH2O (or dry matter) per m² per day", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["gross photosynthesis", "maintenance respiration", "growth respiration", "crop growth rate"], range: ["#2a7f62", "#d9822b", "#c4a35a", "#4a6fa5"]},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(cLong, {x: "DAP", y: "v", stroke: "term", tip: true})]
}), `module2-carbon-balance-${trtName.get(cTrt)}`)
```

```{ojs}
ct = cTot.find(d => d.TRNO === cTrt)
```

Over the season the ${trtName.get(cTrt)} crop fixed ${fmt.int(ct.PHAD)} g CH2O/m² and respired ${fmt.pct(ct["respired share"])} of it (maintenance ${fmt.int(ct.MRAD)}, growth ${fmt.int(ct.GRAD)} g/m²), while the daily crop growth adds up to ${fmt.int(ct.CGRD)} g/m². Respiration is not a small correction: the crop respires almost as much as it
grows.

The way gross photosynthesis is computed is a simulation option. This experiment uses `PHOTO` = `L`, an
hourly leaf-level calculation done in the soil-plant-atmosphere module; with `C` CROPGRO uses a daily
canopy equation instead
([`CROPGRO.for:748-758`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/CROPGRO.for#L748)),
which multiplies a light-limited rate by 0-1 factors for soil fertility (`SLPF`), temperature, leaf N,
water and CO2 ([`PHOTO.for:225`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/PHOTO.for#L225)):

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_g = {} & P_{max} \cdot SLPF \cdot f_{light} \cdot f_{T} \cdot f_{age,N} \\
& \cdot f_{SLW} \cdot f_{CO_2} \cdot f_{LFMAX} \cdot \min(SWFAC,\, f_{O_3})
\end{aligned}
\]

(in the code `PTSMAX`, `SLPF`, `PGFAC`, `TPGFAC`, `E_FAC`, `PGSLW`, `PRATIO`, `PGLFMX` and the minimum of the water
and ozone factors).

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(photo, {header: {treatment: "Treatment", HWAM_L: "Seed yield, PHOTO L", HWAM_C: "Seed yield, PHOTO C", CWAM_L: "Tops, PHOTO L", CWAM_C: "Tops, PHOTO C", obs_HWAM: "Seed yield, observed"}, layout: "auto"})
```

### Where the new mass goes

```{ojs}
viewof pTrt = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Irrigated", 1], ["Rainfed", 2]]), {value: 1, label: "Treatment"})
viewof pMode = Inputs.radio(["kg/ha", "share of tops"], {value: "kg/ha", label: "Show"})
```

```{ojs}
organs = [["LWAD", "leaf"], ["SWAD", "stem"], ["SHAD", "pod shell"], ["GWAD", "seed"]]
pLong = gsim.filter(d => d.TRNO === pTrt).flatMap(d => {
  const tot = d3.sum(organs, ([k]) => d[k] ?? 0);
  return organs.map(([k, n]) => ({DAP: d.DAP, organ: n, v: pMode === "kg/ha" ? (d[k] ?? 0) : tot > 0 ? (d[k] ?? 0) / tot : 0}));
})
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 340, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: pMode === "kg/ha" ? "Dry weight, kg/ha" : "Share of above-ground dry weight", grid: true, tickFormat: pMode === "kg/ha" ? null : "%"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: organs.map(d => d[1]), range: ["#2a7f62", "#9bb8ad", "#c4a35a", "#d9822b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.areaY(pLong, {x: "DAP", y: "v", fill: "organ", order: organs.map(d => d[1]), tip: true}),
    ...(pMode === "kg/ha" ? [Plot.dot(gobs.filter(d => d.TRNO === pTrt), {x: "DAP", y: "CWAD", stroke: "#222", r: 3, tip: true, title: d => `observed tops ${d.CWAD} kg/ha, DAP ${d.DAP}`})] : [])
  ]
}), `module2-partitioning-${trtName.get(pTrt)}`)
```

Until flowering the new mass goes into leaves, stems (and roots, not shown). After the first pods set, a
growing share goes to pods, and late in the season leaves fall and their mass is lost from the tops. The
black dots are the field samples of total tops weight.

Compare any organ with the field samples:


### Light interception

Photosynthesis starts with the light the canopy intercepts. With little leaf area most light reaches the
ground; as leaf area grows, the canopy catches more and more of it, with diminishing returns. The usual summary is Beer's
law,

\[
LI = 1 - e^{-k \cdot LAI},
\]

with an extinction coefficient \(k\). The notebook fits `k`
to the engine's daily light interception (`LI%D`) and LAI by least squares: k = ${lightFit[0].k.toFixed(2)} from ${lightFit[0].days} days. Move the slider to see how `k` shapes the curve.

```{ojs}
viewof kUser = Inputs.range([0.3, 1.2], {step: 0.01, value: 0.5, label: "Your k"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 620), height: 340, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Leaf area index", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Intercepted PAR, %", grid: true, domain: [0, 100]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["engine, irrigated", "engine, rainfed", `fitted k = ${lightFit[0].k.toFixed(2)}`, `your k = ${kUser}`], range: ["#2a7f62", "#d9822b", "#222", "#4a6fa5"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.dot(light, {x: "LAID", y: "LI", fill: d => `engine, ${trtName.get(d.TRNO)}`, r: 2.5, fillOpacity: 0.6, tip: true}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(0, 6.01, 0.05).map(l => [l, 100 * (1 - Math.exp(-lightFit[0].k * l))]), {stroke: () => `fitted k = ${lightFit[0].k.toFixed(2)}`, strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(0, 6.01, 0.05).map(l => [l, 100 * (1 - Math.exp(-kUser * l))]), {stroke: () => `your k = ${kUser}`, strokeWidth: 2, strokeDasharray: "5,3"})
  ]
}), "module2-light-interception")
```

The engine does not use one fixed `k`: the hourly leaf method accounts for the sun's angle and for direct
and diffuse light, which is why the dots scatter around the fitted curve.

### Water stress

`PlantGro` reports two water stress indices: on photosynthesis (`WSPD`) and on expansion, partitioning and
development (`WSGD`). CROPGRO writes them as 1 minus the stress factor
([`Opgrow.for:277-278`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/Opgrow.for#L277)):
0 means no stress. In the rainfed run the expansion index peaks at ${fmt.d2(d3.max(stress.filter(d => d.TRNO === 2), d => d.WSGD))}, the photosynthesis index at ${fmt.d2(d3.max(stress.filter(d => d.TRNO === 2), d => d.WSPD))}:
leaf expansion is the more sensitive process.

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 360, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Stress index (0 = none)", grid: true, domain: [0, 1]},
  fy: {label: null},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["photosynthesis (WSPD)", "expansion (WSGD)", "rain + irrigation, mm/40"], range: ["#d9822b", "#2a7f62", "#9bb8ad"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectY(stress, {x1: "DAP", x2: d => d.DAP + 1, y: d => d.PRED / 40, fy: d => trtName.get(d.TRNO), fill: () => "rain + irrigation, mm/40", tip: true, title: d => `DAP ${d.DAP}: rain ${d.PRED} mm`}),
    Plot.lineY(stress, {x: "DAP", y: "WSPD", fy: d => trtName.get(d.TRNO), stroke: () => "photosynthesis (WSPD)", tip: true}),
    Plot.lineY(stress, {x: "DAP", y: "WSGD", fy: d => trtName.get(d.TRNO), stroke: () => "expansion (WSGD)"})
  ]
}), "module2-water-stress")
```

::: {.source-note}
Rain bars show the weather file's daily rain only (scaled by 1/40). Irrigation of the irrigated treatment is
not drawn; it received ${fmt.int(d3.max(stress.filter(d => d.TRNO === 1), d => d.IRRC))} mm in total.
:::

### The effect of CO2 on growth

Photosynthesis responds to the CO2 concentration of the air, and C3 crops (soybean) more than C4 crops (maize),
whose photosynthesis already concentrates CO2 inside the leaf. The notebook runs the irrigated soybean of UFGA7901
and the irrigated, high-N maize of UFGA8201 at six fixed concentrations, set with the environmental modification
column `ECO2`:

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 640), height: 300, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "CO2, ppm", grid: true},
  y: {label: "Yield relative to 380 ppm", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["soybean (C3)", "maize (C4)"], range: ["#3f7a34", "#f2a33a"]},
  marks: [Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: "#bbb"}), Plot.lineY(co2r, {x: "CO2", y: "relative_yield", stroke: "crop", marker: "dot", tip: true, channels: {"yield, kg/ha": "HWAM", "ET, mm": "ETCM"}})]
}), "module2-co2-response")
```

```{ojs}
co2g = (c, v) => co2r.find(d => d.crop === c && d.CO2 === v).relative_yield
```

From 380 to 700 ppm the soybean yield rises by ${fmt.pct(co2g("soybean (C3)", 700) - 1)}, the maize yield by ${fmt.pct(co2g("maize (C4)", 700) - 1)}.

## 2. Weather data

A DSSAT weather file has a station line (code, latitude, longitude, elevation, `TAV` the mean annual
temperature and `AMP` the amplitude of the monthly mean temperatures) and one line per day with at least
solar radiation (MJ/m²/day), maximum and minimum temperature (°C) and rain (mm). The DSSAT shell's
WeatherMan tool imports, checks and converts such data. In the notebook, pandas and xdssat's `src/wth.py`
do the same.

```{ojs}
viewof wVar = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Temperature", "T"], ["Solar radiation", "SRAD"], ["Rain", "RAIN"]]), {value: "T", label: "Show"})
```

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 300, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {type: "utc", label: "Date, 1979 (soybean season)"},
  y: {label: wVar === "T" ? "°C" : wVar === "SRAD" ? "MJ/m²/day" : "mm/day", grid: true},
  color: wVar === "T" ? {legend: true, domain: ["Tmax", "Tmin"], range: ["#d9822b", "#4a6fa5"]} : undefined,
  marks: wVar === "T" ? [
      Plot.lineY(wSeason, {x: d => new Date(d.date), y: "TMAX", stroke: () => "Tmax", tip: true}),
      Plot.lineY(wSeason, {x: d => new Date(d.date), y: "TMIN", stroke: () => "Tmin", tip: true})]
    : wVar === "SRAD" ? [Plot.lineY(wSeason, {x: d => new Date(d.date), y: "SRAD", stroke: "#c4a35a", tip: true})]
    : [Plot.rectY(wSeason, {x1: d => new Date(d.date), x2: d => new Date(+new Date(d.date) + 864e5), y: "RAIN", fill: "#4a6fa5", tip: true, title: d => `${d3.utcFormat("%d %b")(d.date)}: ${d.RAIN} mm`})]
}), `module2-weather-${wVar}`)
```

### Checks before use

Bad weather data give wrong answers without an error message, so they are checked first. The notebook's
checks on the 1979 file:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(wChecks, {header: {check: "Check", count: "Days"}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(wTavAmp, {header: {what: "Header value", header: "In the file", recomputed: "From the 1979 data"}, layout: "auto"})
```

`TAV` recomputed from the year's own data agrees with the file; `AMP` does not. Both header values are the
ones in the station's long-term climate file, `Weather/Climate/UFGA.CLI` of dssat-csm-data (TAV 20.9, AMP
13.0, "calculated from daily data" for 49 years from 1958): the header carries the long-term climate, not the
year's own values. The engine reads both and uses them for the
soil temperature; it only substitutes defaults (20 and 5 °C) when they are missing
([`weathr.for:215-224`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Weather/weathr.for#L215)).
Checks like the day-to-day change in Tmax list days to look at, not values to delete: a large jump can be
real weather.

### The WeatherMan exercise: weather from Griffin, Georgia

The course's weather exercise hands out the daily records of an experiment station at Griffin, Georgia, as a
spreadsheet, `GRGR-Raw.xls`. It has no header, and its units are not DSSAT's: date as `YYDDD`, rain in inches,
maximum and minimum temperature in °F, solar radiation in cal/cm² per day. The first rows:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(grRaw.slice(0, 8), {header: {YYDDD: "Date (YYDDD)", rain_in: "Rain, in", tmax_F: "Tmax, °F", tmin_F: "Tmin, °F", srad_ly: "Radiation, cal/cm²"}, layout: "auto"})
```

In the DSSAT shell, WeatherMan reads the spreadsheet, is told what each column holds and in which unit,
converts, checks and writes one weather file per year. The notebook does the same with pandas and
`wth.write_wth`, with the station position the exercise gives (33°16' N, 84°17' W, 299 m). Try the
conversions:

```{ojs}
viewof inF = Inputs.number({value: 90, label: "Tmax, °F"})
viewof inIn = Inputs.number({value: 1.2, label: "Rain, inches"})
viewof inLy = Inputs.number({value: 500, label: "Radiation, cal/cm²"})
```

${fmt.d1((inF - 32) * 5 / 9)} °C; ${fmt.d1(inIn * 25.4)} mm; ${fmt.d1(inLy * 0.04184)} MJ/m²/day
(°C = (°F - 32) × 5/9; 1 inch = 25.4 mm; 1 cal/cm² = 0.04184 MJ/m²).

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(grChecks, {header: {check: "Check on the converted data", count: "Days"}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
grCheckText = d3.sum(grChecks.slice(1), d => d.count) === 0 ? "The checks find nothing to repair in this record." : "Some checks flag days; the notebook fills them as described there."
Inputs.table(grFiles, {header: {file: "File written", days: "Days", first: "From", last: "To"},
  format: {first: d => d3.utcFormat("%Y-%m-%d")(d), last: d => d3.utcFormat("%Y-%m-%d")(d)}, layout: "auto"})
```

${grCheckText} The header of every file carries the

### Converting back and forth: an optional column matters

The notebook also converts the 1979 Gainesville file to those units and back, writes a new DSSAT weather file
with `wth.write_wth`, and reruns the soybean experiment:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(wRound, {header: {variable: "Quantity", value: "Value"}, format: {value: d => d >= 100 ? fmt.int(d) : d.toFixed(2)}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
rt = Object.fromEntries(wRound.map(d => [d.variable, d.value]))
```

Rain differs by up to ${rt["RAIN, largest change"]} mm because the inches were rounded to two decimals.
The more instructive result is the last pair of rows. The original file also has a `PAR` column
(photosynthetically active radiation). When the conversion drops it, the engine estimates PAR from solar
radiation instead, and irrigated seed yield changes from ${fmt.int(rt["seed yield irrigated, original file"])}
to ${fmt.int(rt["seed yield irrigated, converted, no PAR"])} kg/ha. An optional column can matter as much as a
units error.

### When there are no daily records: weather generators

A weather generator draws daily maximum and minimum temperature, solar radiation and rain that are statistically
like a site's climate. DSSAT has two: WGEN, which needs at least 5 years of daily data, and SIMMETEO, which works
from monthly means (the course's weather lecture). Their parameters sit in a climate file, one per site, named
`IIss.CLI` (here `UFGA.CLI`). The `WTHER` option of the simulation controls chooses: `M` and `G` read the
weather from a file, and `S` and `W` let the engine generate it itself from SIMMETEO or WGEN inputs
([`Weather/weathr.for:575-577`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Weather/weathr.for#L575)).
Generated weather fills gaps and lets one run many seasons where few were measured; it is how the
[seasonal analysis of module 5](module5.qmd) and the [rotations of module 6](module6.qmd) get decades of weather.
It is not a forecast: each generated season is one draw of the climate, not of a particular year.

### What if the weather were different?

Each scenario edits the weather file and reruns both treatments.


```{ojs}
      tip: true, channels: {"seed yield, kg/ha": "HWAM", "maturity, DAP": "maturity_dap"}}),
```

```{ojs}

warmText = {
  const a = ws["temperature +4 °C"].maturity_dap, b = ws["baseline"].maturity_dap;
```

For the ${wsTrt} crop, 20% less radiation costs ${fmt.pct(-ws["SRAD x 0.8"].change)} of seed yield, and 4 °C warmer weather costs ${fmt.pct(-ws["temperature +4 °C"].change)}. ${warmText} Halving the rain costs the rainfed crop ${fmt.pct(-wSens.find(d => d.treatment === "rainfed" && d.scenario === "rain x 0.5").change)}, the irrigated crop ${fmt.pct(-wSens.find(d => d.treatment === "irrigated" && d.scenario === "rain x 0.5").change)}: its
irrigation was a fixed schedule, not refilled as needed.

## 3. The minimum data set and the file system

A DSSAT run needs a **minimum data set**: the site and its soil, daily weather, the crop management, and the
crop's coefficients [@hunt1998]. The same reference sets out levels of data beyond that minimum: what is enough to
run the model is not enough to calibrate it, and calibrating needs less than a full evaluation, which also needs
measurements during the season.

The course's lecture on the minimum data set put these as three levels, each adding to the one before:

| Level | Needed for | Data |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Running the model | Daily weather (maximum and minimum temperature, rain, solar radiation); soil surface and profile (water limits, nitrogen, organic matter); management (crop, cultivar, planting date, spacing, irrigation, fertilizer, other operations) |
| 2 | Calibrating and evaluating it | Level 1, plus crop measurements (yield and its components, flowering and maturity dates, growth samples during the season) and soil measurements (water, nitrogen and carbon by depth over time) |
| 3 | Developing it | Levels 1 and 2, plus detailed experiments on the response to temperature, water, nitrogen and other factors |

Level 1 is what DSSAT, following IBSNAT, calls *the* minimum data set. Modules 1 and 2 run on it; module 3
(calibration) and module 4 (measurement files) need level 2.

Each part of the data lives in its own text file. The base run used these:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(files, {header: {file: "File", role: "What it holds", lines: "Lines", source: "From"}, layout: "auto"})
```

Experiment files are named `IIssYYnn.ccX`:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(naming, {header: {part: "Part of UFGA7901.SBX", value: "Value"}, layout: "auto"})
```

with `A` and `T` instead of `X` for the observed data; the weather file uses the same first eight characters
and `.WTH`. DSSAT ships ${d3.sum(exps, d => d.experiments)} such experiment files in ${exps.length} folders;
the folders with most are:

```{ojs}
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 380, marginLeft: 110,
  x: {label: "Experiment files (FileX) in dssat-csm-data", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  marks: [Plot.barX(exps.slice(0, 20), {y: "folder", x: "experiments", fill: d => d.folder === "Soybean" ? "#d9822b" : "#2a7f62", sort: {y: "-x"}, tip: true})]
}), "module2-experiments-per-crop")
```

## 4. Species, ecotype and cultivar coefficients

CROPGRO reads its crop parameters at three levels. The **species** file (`SBGRO048.SPE`) holds what all
soybeans share, such as cardinal temperatures and the photosynthesis and respiration parameters. The
**ecotype** file (`SBGRO048.ECO`) groups cultivars, here by maturity group. The **cultivar** file
(`SBGRO048.CUL`) holds the coefficients that users estimate for each variety.

### Day length and flowering

Soybean is a short-day plant: development toward flowering slows when days are longer than a critical day
length `CSDL`. `PPSEN` is how fast it slows per hour beyond that. The engine computes the relative rate with
an "inverse linear" curve
([`UTILS.for:378-383`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Utilities/UTILS.for#L378),
called in [`PHENOL.for:243`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/PHENOL.for#L243)):
rate 1 up to `CSDL`, then falling in a straight line to the ecotype's minimum `THVAR`:

\[
\begin{gathered}
f(DL) =
\begin{cases}
1 & DL \le CSDL \\
1 - (1 - THVAR)\,\dfrac{DL - CSDL}{CLDL - CSDL} & \text{in between} \\
THVAR & DL \ge CLDL
\end{cases} \\[6pt]
CLDL = CSDL + \frac{1 - THVAR}{PPSEN}
\end{gathered}
\]

with \(DL\) the day length in hours
([`Ipphenol.for:239-240`](https://github.com/DSSAT/dssat-csm-os/blob/25c93b9a2f73f8ec45bf441b198dac5fb7b22849/Plant/CROPGRO/Ipphenol.for#L239)).
`THVAR` is ${bragg.THVAR} for every soybean ecotype in the file, so development stops entirely at that day length.

```{ojs}
viewof ppCul = Inputs.select(cultivars.map(d => d.var), {value: "IB0001", label: "Start from", format: v => { const c = cultivars.find(d => d.var === v); return `${c.name.trim()} (CSDL ${c.CSDL}, PPSEN ${c.PPSEN})`; }})
```

```{ojs}
ppStart = cultivars.find(d => d.var === ppCul)
viewof csdl = Inputs.range([11, 15], {step: 0.01, value: ppStart.CSDL, label: "CSDL, h"})
viewof ppsen = Inputs.range([0.1, 0.5], {step: 0.005, value: ppStart.PPSEN, label: "PPSEN, 1/h"})
```

```{ojs}
function ppRate(dayl, c, p, thvar = 0) {
  const x2 = c + (1 - thvar) / Math.max(p, 1e-6);
  if (dayl <= c) return 1;
  if (dayl >= x2) return thvar;
  return 1 - (1 - thvar) * (dayl - c) / (x2 - c);
}
dlRange = d3.extent(daylength, d => d.DAYLD)
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(W, 640), height: 320, marginLeft: 55,
  x: {label: "Day length, hours", domain: [11, 16], grid: true},
  y: {label: "Relative rate of development to flowering", domain: [0, 1.05], grid: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([dlRange], {x1: d => d[0], x2: d => d[1], fill: "#c4a35a", fillOpacity: 0.25}),
    Plot.text([dlRange], {x: d => (d[0] + d[1]) / 2, y: 0.08, text: () => "Gainesville, Apr-Nov 1979", fill: "#806a2a"}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(11, 16.01, 0.02).map(x => [x, ppRate(x, csdl, ppsen, bragg.THVAR)]), {stroke: "#2a7f62", strokeWidth: 2.5, tip: true}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(11, 16.01, 0.02).map(x => [x, ppRate(x, ppStart.CSDL, ppStart.PPSEN, bragg.THVAR)]), {stroke: "#999", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})
  ]
}), "module2-photoperiod-response")
```

The shaded band is the range of day length at Gainesville from April to November 1979 (from the engine's
weather output). Dashed: the cultivar you started from. In the generic maturity groups of the cultivar file,
`CSDL` falls from ${cultivars[0].CSDL} h (group 000) to ${cultivars.find(d => d.var === "990010").CSDL} h (group 10). A cultivar whose `CSDL` is above the longest Gainesville day is not slowed
at all; Bragg, with ${bragg.CSDL} h, is slowed for much of the summer.

### Coefficients across the crop models

Every crop model has its own cultivar coefficients. CERES models describe a cultivar mainly by thermal time to
stages and by grain number and size; CROPGRO models by photothermal days between reproductive stages and by leaf,
pod and seed traits. The definitions below are read from the comment block of each model's cultivar file in the
engine:

```{ojs}
viewof cmModel = Inputs.select([...new Set(coefModels.map(d => d.model_name))], {value: "CROPGRO-Soybean", label: "Crop model"})
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(coefModels.filter(d => d.model_name === cmModel), {columns: ["coefficient", "definition"],
  header: {coefficient: "Coefficient", definition: "Definition (from the cultivar file)"}, layout: "auto", rows: 20, width: {definition: 620}})
```

CERES-Rice's `TCLDF`, the temperature below which cold makes spikelets sterile, is the coefficient the
[rice case study](../java/science.qmd) raises for the cool highlands of Java.

### Maturity group and planting date

Generic maturity groups 3, 5 and 7, and Bragg, each planted every three weeks from 10 April, under potential
production (water and N switched off), all in one FileX:

Maturity group 7 flowers ${d3.max(mgLate, d => d.R1_dap)} days after a May planting but only ${d3.min(mgLate, d => d.R1_dap)} days after the August one. The day length at planting is ${fmt.d1(mgLate[2].daylength_at_planting)} h in late May and ${fmt.d1(mgLate[mgLate.length - 1].daylength_at_planting)} h in mid August, and falling: a late crop spends the weeks before flowering in

### One coefficient at a time: the course's values

Exercise 3 of the course changes one coefficient of the maturity group 7 cultivar (`990007`) at a time, to the
values the course gives, in the irrigated treatment. Every value is a separate cultivar in a copy of the cultivar
file (`learnlib.write_cultivar_variants`), so the whole sweep is one FileX and one engine call. Exercise 4 adds a
new cultivar, `DS0001`: maturity group 7 with `PODUR` = 7.

```{ojs}
coefDesc = new Map([["EM-FL", "emergence to first flower, photothermal days"], ["SFDUR", "seed filling duration of a pod cohort, photothermal days"],
  ["PODUR", "time to reach the final pod load, photothermal days"], ["WTPSD", "maximum weight per seed, g"],
  ["CSDL", "critical short day length, h (12.33 to 12.07: MG 7 to MG 8)"], ["PPSEN", "photoperiod sensitivity, 1/h (0.32 to 0.33: MG 7 to MG 8)"]])
viewof cPick = Inputs.radio([...coefDesc.keys()], {value: "SFDUR", label: "Coefficient", format: k => `${k} (${coefDesc.get(k)})`})
viewof cgVar = Inputs.select(new Map([["Seed weight, kg/ha", "GWAD"], ["Weight per seed, mg", "GWGD"], ["Seed number, per m²", "G#AD"], ["Pod number, per m²", "P#AD"],
  ["Harvest index", "HIAD"], ["Shelling %", "SH%D"], ["Leaf area index", "LAID"], ["Tops weight, kg/ha", "CWAD"]]), {value: "GWAD", label: "Variable"})
```

```{ojs}
cRows = sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === cPick || d.coefficient === "standard MG 7")
cLabels = cRows.map(d => d.label)
withDownload(Plot.plot({
  width: W, height: 340, marginLeft: 60,
  x: {label: "Days after planting", grid: true},
  y: {label: cgVar, grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: cLabels, scheme: "viridis"},
  marks: [Plot.lineY(sensCoefG.filter(d => cLabels.includes(d.label)), {x: "DAP", y: cgVar, stroke: "label", strokeWidth: d => d.label === "standard MG 7" ? 3 : 1.5, tip: true})]
}), `module2-${cPick}-${cgVar.replace(/[^A-Z]/gi, "")}`)
```

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === cPick || d.coefficient === "standard MG 7" || (cPick === "PODUR" && d.coefficient === "new cultivar")),
  {columns: ["label", "R1_dap", "maturity_dap", "HWAM", "seed_number", "seed_mg", "HIAM", "LAIX"],
   header: {label: "Run", R1_dap: "First flower, DAP", maturity_dap: "Maturity, DAP", HWAM: "Seed yield, kg/ha", seed_number: "Seeds per m²", seed_mg: "Seed size, mg", HIAM: "Harvest index", LAIX: "Max LAI"},
   format: {seed_mg: fmt.int, HIAM: d => d.toFixed(2), LAIX: d => d.toFixed(1)}, layout: "auto"})
```

```{ojs}
sensRange = [...coefDesc.keys()].map(k => {
  const g = sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === k || d.coefficient === "standard MG 7");
  return {coefficient: k, R1: d3.max(g, d => d.R1_dap) - d3.min(g, d => d.R1_dap), maturity: d3.max(g, d => d.maturity_dap) - d3.min(g, d => d.maturity_dap),
          yield: d3.max(g, d => d.HWAM) - d3.min(g, d => d.HWAM), seeds: d3.max(g, d => d.seed_number) - d3.min(g, d => d.seed_number), size: d3.max(g, d => d.seed_mg) - d3.min(g, d => d.seed_mg)};
})
podur7 = sensCoef.find(d => d.coefficient === "PODUR" && d.value === 7)
ds1 = sensCoef.find(d => d.coefficient === "new cultivar")
wt = sensCoef.filter(d => d.coefficient === "WTPSD")
```

Across the course's values (including the standard MG 7), each coefficient moves these outputs by:

```{ojs}
Inputs.table(sensRange, {header: {coefficient: "Coefficient", R1: "First flower, days", maturity: "Maturity, days", yield: "Seed yield, kg/ha", seeds: "Seeds per m²", size: "Seed size, mg"},
  format: {yield: fmt.int, seeds: fmt.int, size: fmt.int}, layout: "auto"})
```

`EM-FL`, `CSDL` and `PPSEN` move the dates, which is why calibration (module 3) sets them first, from observed
flowering and maturity. `SFDUR` leaves the dates alone and changes how long each pod cohort fills, so seed yield
follows it. `WTPSD` is the exercise's puzzle: from ${wt[0].value} to ${wt[wt.length - 1].value} g the seeds grow from ${fmt.int(wt[0].seed_mg)} to ${fmt.int(wt[wt.length - 1].seed_mg)} mg, but the seed number falls from ${fmt.int(wt[0].seed_number)} to ${fmt.int(wt[wt.length - 1].seed_number)} per m² and the yield hardly changes. The new cultivar `DS0001` gives ${fmt.int(ds1.HWAM)} kg/ha with ${fmt.int(ds1.seed_number)} seeds per m², the same as the `PODUR` = 7 run (${fmt.int(podur7.HWAM)} kg/ha): the exercise's self test, that a cultivar entry with a changed coefficient behaves like the
sensitivity run with that coefficient.

## From one field to a grid: xdssat

Module 2 wrote weather files for one station. For a region, xdssat writes one weather file per 0.1° cell, from the
gridded AgERA5 data set, derived from the ERA5 reanalysis [@agera5], and the same checks and conversions apply to every cell. The season
weather of irrigated wet-season rice in the [rice case study](../java/index.qmd), averaged over 1991-2020:

```{ojs}
import {cellFeatures, adminMarks} from "../assets/js/dl.js"
gCells = FileAttachment("../java/data/grid_cells.csv").csv({typed: true})
gOutline = FileAttachment("../java/data/java_outline.geojson").json()
gProv = FileAttachment("../java/data/provinces.geojson").json()
gDist = FileAttachment("../java/data/districts.geojson").json()
gSummary = FileAttachment("../java/data/summary.json").json()
gMapW = Math.min(width, 960)
```


## Self-test

1. Respiration took about 40% of gross photosynthesis. Would you expect that share to be higher or lower in a
   hotter climate, and why?
2. Why do the irrigated and rainfed treatments of UFGA7901 yield almost the same?
3. Your weather data lack PAR. Is that an error? What does the engine do, and how large was the effect here?
4. Bragg (CSDL 12.33 h) is grown in Java, at about 7° S, where day length changes little over the year.
   Use the day-length chart to predict its time to flowering compared with Gainesville in June, then test
   it in the notebook.
5. Which observation would you use to estimate `WTPSD`, and why not seed yield?
